explanations.explanation: Verse 30 puts it in order. As soon as Laban, Rebekah's brother, saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister's wrists, and heard her words, he went and found the man. I think a brother who spots jewelry on his sister's wrists is going to get moving. Ring first, then he goes to find the man.

Hold on, baker, this one is True. Verse 30 says that as soon as Laban, Rebekah's brother, saw the ring, and the bracelets on his sister's wrists, and heard Rebekah's words, he went and found the man standing by the camels near the spring. Jewelry first, then the brother shows up. I think that's the fastest anyone has ever gone from 'nice bracelet' to 'who is this guy?'
Laban says, “Come, you who are blessed by the LORD…” (verse 31). That's how he greets a stranger standing out by a spring with his camels. Not a bad welcome for a man who just showed up.
No king is mentioned in this welcome. Laban says, “Come, you who are blessed by the LORD…” (verse 31). The man is Abraham's servant, and Laban calls him blessed by the LORD.
Laban never calls him that. In verse 31 he says, “Come, you who are blessed by the LORD…” Then he asks why the man is standing out in the open when a house is ready.
It's actually the opposite. Laban says, “I have prepared the house and a place for the camels.” (verse 31). Everything is ready before the servant even steps inside. Laban is not scrambling.

Right, the opposite is true. Laban says, “Why are you standing out here? I have prepared the house and a place for the camels.” (verse 31). The house is ready before the man says a word about why he came. Then the camels are unloaded, and straw and feed are brought to them (verse 32). I think Laban would pass any surprise-guest test.

The servant does it the other way around. Verse 33 says a meal was set before him, but he said, “I will not eat until I have told you what I came to say.” The food sits there while he talks. I'd have trouble with that, honestly.

He holds off. The meal is right in front of him, and he says, “I will not eat until I have told you what I came to say.” (verse 33). Laban answers, “Please speak.” The talking comes first and the eating comes after.

The servant says, “…my master has given him everything he owns.” (verse 36). Abraham's wife Sarah had a son in her old age, and that's Isaac, the one the servant is finding a wife for. Everything is a whole lot more than half.
The servant doesn't say half of anything. In verse 36 he says Abraham “…has given him everything he owns.” The son is Isaac, born to Abraham's wife Sarah in her old age.
A house isn't what the servant mentions. Verse 36 says Abraham “…has given him everything he owns.” That's the son Sarah had in her old age, and the whole estate is his.

explanations.answer: To his father's house and family
explanations.explanation: Abraham told his servant, “…you shall go to my father’s house and to my kindred to take a wife for my son.” (verse 38). The Canaanites were ruled out, so family was the direction. That's exactly where the servant ends up, at Rebekah's family.

explanations.answer: To the great cities of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt never comes up here. Verse 38 says, “…you shall go to my father’s house and to my kindred to take a wife for my son.” The servant is sent to Abraham's own family.

explanations.answer: To the towns along the Jordan
explanations.explanation: No Jordan towns in this part of the story. Abraham's words in verse 38 are, “…you shall go to my father’s house and to my kindred…” Family is where the servant was told to look.

Verse 41 has it. Abraham says, “…if they refuse to give her to you, then you will be released from my oath.” The servant isn't stuck forever if the answer is no. He's also telling Rebekah's family this up front, which is honest of him.
Abraham did say it. In verse 41 he tells his servant, “…if they refuse to give her to you, then you will be released from my oath.” So a no from the family would let the servant go free of the oath.

The servant says, “Whose daughter are you?” (verse 47). She answers, “The daughter of Bethuel son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.” Bethuel is her father. Only then does he put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her wrists.
That question isn't in the servant's telling. In verse 47 he asks, “Whose daughter are you?” Rebekah answers with her father, Bethuel, and her grandfather, Nahor.

Ooh, good guess, friend, but nobody asks for a name here. In verse 47 the servant asks, “Whose daughter are you?” Rebekah answers, “The daughter of Bethuel son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.” So he's asking about her family, and only after that do the ring and bracelets go on. Her answer tells him who her people are, and that's what he came to find out.
The servant says, “…if not, let me know, so that I may go elsewhere.” (verse 49). He asks for a plain answer, yes or no. Either way, he's ready to move on.
Waiting at the spring isn't his plan. He says, “…if not, let me know, so that I may go elsewhere.” (verse 49). He's asking for a clear answer so he knows what to do next.
He never talks about sending for Abraham. Verse 49 says, “…if not, let me know, so that I may go elsewhere.” He'd just go somewhere else.
Laban and Bethuel answer, “This is from the LORD; we have no choice in the matter.” (verse 50). Bethuel is Rebekah's father. They say it came from the LORD, not from the servant or anyone else.
They don't say Abraham. In verse 50, Laban and Bethuel answer, “This is from the LORD; we have no choice in the matter.” Abraham is the servant's master, but the LORD is who they name.
Nahor is named earlier as Rebekah's grandfather (verse 47), but not here. Laban and Bethuel say, “This is from the LORD; we have no choice in the matter.” (verse 50). They credit the LORD.

Verse 53 says he brought out jewels of silver and gold, and articles of clothing, and gave them to Rebekah. He also gave precious gifts to her brother and her mother. Rebekah's gifts get named first, though. Silver, gold AND clothing? I'd need a second mustache just to carry that much!
It's actually True. Verse 53 says the servant brought out jewels of silver and gold, and articles of clothing, and gave them to Rebekah. He also gave precious gifts to her brother and her mother.

explanations.answer: A little more time with her
explanations.explanation: Her brother and mother say, “Let the girl remain with us ten days or so. After that, she may go.” (verse 55). They aren't saying no. They're asking for a little more time before she leaves.

Gifts for her father? Not in this scene, friend. Her brother and mother say, “Let the girl remain with us ten days or so. After that, she may go.” (verse 55). The gifts here go to Rebekah, her brother and her mother (verse 53). What they're asking for is TIME.
They don't ask for Abraham to come. Verse 55 has them saying, “Let the girl remain with us ten days or so. After that, she may go.” What they ask for is time.
He doesn't agree. He says, “Do not delay me, since the LORD has made my journey a success. Send me on my way so that I may go to my master.” (verse 56). Ten days or so is not what he asks for.
He holds his ground. In verse 56 he replies, “Do not delay me, since the LORD has made my journey a success.” Then he adds, “Send me on my way so that I may go to my master.”

explanations.answer: She will go with the man
explanations.explanation: They ask, “Will you go with this man?” and she answers, “I will go…” (verse 58). The servant wants to leave now and her family wants ten days or so, and Rebekah is the one asked. Her answer is short and clear.
That was her brother and mother's request (verse 55). When they call Rebekah and ask, she says, “I will go…” (verse 58). She doesn't ask for the ten days.
Her family says, “We will call the girl and ask her opinion.” (verse 57). So Rebekah answers for herself. Her words in verse 58 are, “I will go…”

explanations.answer: To be the mother of thousands
explanations.explanation: They say, “Our sister, may you become the mother of thousands upon thousands.” (verse 60). That's the first part of their blessing. They go on to bless her offspring too.

explanations.answer: To come back home again soon
explanations.explanation: Coming home soon isn't part of the blessing. In verse 60 they say, “Our sister, may you become the mother of thousands upon thousands.” Then they speak over her offspring.

explanations.answer: To be rich in land and gold
explanations.explanation: Land and gold aren't in their words. Verse 60 says, “Our sister, may you become the mother of thousands upon thousands. May your offspring possess the gates of their enemies.” The silver and gold came earlier, from the servant's gifts (verse 53). The blessing is about her children.
Verse 61 says Rebekah and her servant girls got ready, mounted the camels, and followed the man. Then the servant took Rebekah and left. She doesn't leave alone.

Hold on, this one is True. Verse 61 says Rebekah and her servant girls got ready, mounted the camels, and followed the man. So she isn't heading out on her own. Her servant girls go right along with her on those camels, and the servant takes her and leaves.

Verse 63 says Isaac, Abraham's son, went out to the field to meditate, and looking up, he saw the camels approaching. Those are the camels carrying Rebekah and her servant girls. I'd say that's quite the evening view.
No sheep in this verse. Isaac, Abraham's son, looks up in the field and sees the camels approaching (verse 63). Rebekah is on one of them.
No soldiers here. When Isaac, Abraham's son, looks up from his time in the field, he sees the camels approaching (verse 63). That's Rebekah's group arriving, and it's a peaceful sight.
Verse 65 says, “So she took her veil and covered herself.” She had asked the servant who the man in the field was, and he said, “It is my master…” Her veil comes out as she learns it's Isaac.

The jar belongs to the spring scene, where she carried it on her shoulder (verse 45). Here, verse 65 says, “So she took her veil and covered herself.” Just before that, she has gotten down from her camel (verse 64) and asked who that man in the field is (verse 65). So no jar this time, just a veil.

A staff? Not this time, friend! Rebekah gets down from her camel (verse 64) and asks who the man in the field is. After the servant says, “It is my master…” verse 65 says, “So she took her veil and covered herself.” The veil is the one the text names. That's the answer this blank is looking for.

Verse 67 says, “And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother’s death.” His mother was Sarah, and Isaac brought Rebekah into her tent. I think this is a tender line, so let's let it be tender.
Honored isn't the word the text uses. Verse 67 says Isaac loved Rebekah and “…was comforted after his mother’s death.” His mother was Sarah, and Rebekah came into her tent.
The text doesn't say rewarded. It says Isaac loved Rebekah and “…was comforted after his mother’s death.” (verse 67). His mother was Sarah, and this is a quiet, tender moment.
